title: Love
hookLine: the greatest virtue, the one that lasts (1 Corinthians 13:13)

cards: The church in Corinth was arguing. Early in Paul's first letter to them, he says word has reached him that there are contentions among them. Some say they follow Paul, some Apollos, some Peter.

Later in the letter they're comparing spiritual gifts: who speaks in tongues, who prophesies, whose gift matters more. And right in the middle of that quarrel, Paul stops and writes the passage on love.

It wasn't written for a candlelit ceremony. It was written to a room full of people who were tired of each other. Day 89 met it as love is patient; today, the third virtue, the one Paul calls the greatest.

teach.b: Open the King James Bible to that chapter and you won't find the word love. You'll find charity. "Charity suffereth long, and is kind; charity envieth not; charity vaunteth not itself, is not puffed up."
The old Latin Bible, the Vulgate, has caritas in the same place, and that's today's word. In the Greek Paul wrote, it's agape. Whatever the language, Paul doesn't define love as a feeling.
He describes it as behavior: patient, kind, not jealous, not showing off. Some readers hear each line aimed at a Corinthian habit.
Then he says the thing that gives love its place above the others: "Charity never faileth." Prophecies will end, he says. Knowledge will pass.
And the chapter closes: "And now abideth faith, hope, charity, these three; but the greatest of these is charity." Why the greatest? Paul doesn't spell it out, and readers have offered reasons.
One old reading goes like this: faith will one day see what it trusted, and hope will one day have what it waited for, but love has nowhere further to go. It simply continues. That's today's line.
And because love is behavior, it has to land somewhere.
The first letter of John says it plainly: "let us not love in word, neither in tongue; but in deed and in truth."
Caritas isn't proved in a speech. It's proved in a dish washed, a call returned, a grudge not mentioned.

how: Some Christians choose 1 Corinthians 13 for weddings and funerals, and churches in different traditions teach love of God and neighbor as the heart of Christian life, shown in works of mercy and everyday kindness.

s: Paul wrote the love chapter for a wedding
he wrote it to a church full of contentions, in the middle of a letter about their quarrels.
the King James Bible says charity where a reader today might expect love
Paul describes love mainly as a feeling
he describes behavior: patient, kind, not envious, not puffed up.

games.q: you're Paul. the church in Corinth is split over leaders and comparing spiritual gifts. how do you answer them?
o: rank the gifts so they know which matters most.
write to them about love, which never fails.
tell them to split into separate churches.
games.why: in the middle of the letter he turns to love, and ends: "the greatest of these is charity."

practice: Bring one person to mind, ideally someone a little tiring, the way the Corinthians were tiring to each other, and walk through Paul's lines with them in view: patient, where could you wait for them; kind, what one kind thing would actually help?
Pick one deed, small and specific. If you pray, you can pray for them by name.

wordCard.voice: Caritas. The Latin word for the love in Paul's chapter, charity in the King James: patient, kind, shown in deeds, and the one that never fails.

orig.note: Latin: the word in the old Latin Bible's 1 Corinthians 13, where the Greek has agapē.

carryVoice: Your line: love lasts. The deed can stay quiet, and it still counts. See you tomorrow.
